entities.summary:
Jörg von Halsbach (c. 1450–1488), known also as Jörg Halspach or Ganghofer, was a pivotal German master builder and architect whose innovative use of brick construction profoundly shaped the urban landscape of late 15th-century Bavaria. Originating from Polling near Weilheim, Halsbach established his reputation primarily through his extensive work in the ducal cities of Munich and Freising, where his designs represented a sophisticated blend of late Gothic tradition and emerging Renaissance sensibilities. His short but impactful career left an indelible mark on religious and civic architecture, particularly through his mastery of intricate vaulting techniques and robust brick structures, which contrasted with the prevailing stone-centric construction of the era, showcasing an early adoption of cost-effective and structurally resilient materials.

Halsbach's most celebrated achievement is the Frauenkirche (Cathedral Church of Our Lady) in Munich, commissioned by Duke Sigismund and Duke Albert IV. Construction began in 1468 under another master, but Halsbach took over in 1470, completing the substantial brick edifice by 1488, the year of his death. He designed its distinctive 99-meter-high onion domes, though these were only added in 1525, based on his original plans. His work also includes significant contributions to the Old Town Hall in Munich, particularly its impressive tower, and the redesign of the Freising Cathedral, where he implemented advanced vaulting solutions. He likely contributed to other structures such as St. Peter's Church in Munich and the parish church of St. Michael in Polling, demonstrating a consistent aesthetic across multiple commissions.
